title: What can we do to minimise Cognitive Overload?
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton builds on his earlier definition of cognitive overload by asking what schools can do about it. He sets out four short stories of overload affecting a sarcastic-teacher victim, a confused young child, a harassed teacher and a stressed parent, and asks what could have eased each. He then shows how the earlier factors of evidence, curriculum, shared agreement about the kind of students being developed, and structures and systems can raise or lower overload. Finally he explains schemas as personal big pictures that chunk many items into one, and notes they can be unhelpful as easily as helpful. He ends with a checklist for teachers, leaders and parents.
points: Overload affects students, teachers and parents alike, and it often arrives before any planned learning starts.
Overloaded curricula and unfocused evidence systems raise the load on everyone, while learning-focused systems reduce it.
Schemas let working memory treat many items as one, so building helpful schemas is a way of lightening load.
A key task of school leadership is reducing teachers' overload so they have energy for learners.
quotes: We started last week’s post with Dylan William’s quote that cognitive overload is ‘the single most important thing for teachers to know about’. That’s because it’s the factor that affects learning that is itself most affected by all of the other factors that affect learning.

I haven’t worked through this yet but it does seem to me that there are links between ‘schemas’ and what we have been calling understanding. Schemas are personal to us, based on our repeated experiences and they underpin how we approach what happens to us that is new.

A schema is something that is laid down as a result of our experiences. As we process those experiences, commonalities and differences reveal themselves and cluster around related items. Slowly, over time, we come to see a big picture that becomes so sticky that a) it underpins how we make sense of the world and b) our brains treat it as one ‘bit’ of information rather than the many multiple ‘bits’ it actually contains.

When this happens, our working memory is speeded up because a) not everything is being processed as new and b) each new ‘bit’ that we process has chance to fit into the overarching big picture. It’s a little like a jigsaw that gets easier the more pieces are in the right place.

Schemas begin to be created when children are very young. It is thought that one of the reasons young children are so at ease with repetitively stacking bricks or containers over time - and many other similar activities - is that it is helping them build simple schemas.

It’s worth saying that schemas, like learning of which they are a part, are not good in themselves. We build unhelpful schemas in the same way as we build helpful ones. We need to remember that the brain doesn’t care.
